claims.text: Parts procurement discount for a single-location independent collision repair shop is approximately 22% off list price, versus approximately 25% off list for a small multi-shop operator (3 shops, ~$9M revenue), representing a 3-percentage-point spread on all parts spend.
claims.evidence: Focus Advisors, the leading collision repair M&A advisory, explicitly quantified this discount differential in a 2024 article on MSO value creation: 'Buying parts at 25% off instead of 22%... all add up to reduced overhead per shop.' This is the most directly sourced documented reference point for procurement cost differential between independent and MSO tiers. Parts represent approximately 34–39% of total revenue in collision repair, so this 3pp spread translates to approximately 105–117 basis points of EBITDA improvement at the small MSO threshold.

citations.title: Growing the Independent MSO: Create More Value by Scaling Up – Focus Advisors Automotive
citations.content_snippet: Buying parts at 25% off instead of 22%, paint discounts increasing from 50% to 60%, spreading out the management costs, training, rent factors, insurance, marketing and a host of other small costs all add up to reduced overhead per shop. As an illustrative example, a $3 million single-shop might generate a 9% EBITDA margin, whereas a medium-sized 3-shop MSO might generate closer to a 14% EBITDA margin.

caveats: Focus Advisors is an M&A advisory with an incentive to promote MSO value creation; figures may be optimistic or illustrative rather than audited
The discount level for 500+ location platforms is not documented in any publicly available source — the 22→25% reference covers only the single-shop to small-MSO transition
DRP agreements may require shops to share procurement savings with insurers via lower blended claim costs, so EBITDA capture rate may be lower than gross savings

claims.text: LKQ Corporation's recycled (salvage) parts sell for 25–50% less than OEM equivalents, and its aftermarket parts (new, third-party manufactured) can be 50–70% less than OEM, providing collision repair chains a material alternative-parts cost lever that independents access at similar absolute prices but at lower committed-volume terms.
claims.evidence: LKQ Corporation, the dominant alternative parts supplier for collision repair chains in North America with $5.76B in North American wholesale revenue in 2024, publicly states recycled parts cost 25–50% below OEM and aftermarket parts cost 50–70% below OEM. However, these discounts are relative to OEM list price — not relative to what any shop pays for OEM parts. Large chains benefit from higher committed volumes through LKQ's national network. The parts mix in collision repair is approximately 62% OEM, 22% aftermarket, and 10% recycled, so the largest cost-reduction lever remains OEM procurement, not LKQ pricing.

claims.text: OEM dealer parts are sold to wholesale collision repair accounts at approximately 10–15% above the dealer's own wholesale cost (i.e., 10–15% above what the dealer paid the manufacturer), which is typically 30–40% below dealer list price — giving shops an effective OEM parts cost of roughly 15–30% below published list price regardless of chain size.
claims.evidence: Industry sources confirm the dealer OEM parts supply chain: dealers purchase from manufacturers at 30–40% below list and sell to wholesale accounts (repair shops) at 10–15% above their wholesale cost. This means any shop — independent or chain — accessing OEM parts through the standard dealer-wholesale channel pays roughly 15–30% below list. Large chains negotiate beyond this floor through volume commitments and preferred dealer relationships, but the baseline discount is broadly available, limiting the incremental advantage of scale on OEM procurement to the margin above this floor.

citations.title: Dealer Repair Parts Pricing Secrets – Tundra Headquarters Blog

Dealers sell parts to wholesale customers (like independent repair shops) for 10–15% over wholesale — which is significantly less than retail.

The downside reflects: (a) Romans Group documented 7–10% claims decline in 2024–2025; (b) Boyd's 9.1% EBITDA decline on 1.8% SS sales decline, implying 5x operating leverage; (c) rising capex requirements for ADAS equipment ($500K/location). Shops with extensive OEM certifications can now command 6.5x EBITDA multiples, while volume-driven MSOs are stuck at 3x–4.5x. Investors are rewarding specialization over size. The failure of traditional consolidation models reveals a fundamental misread of what collision repair demands in 2025 and beyond.

caveats: The OEM-certified vs. volume-MSO multiple comparison may reflect selection bias: only the best-operated specialty shops survive to transact, while struggling volume MSOs may also trade below 3x
Quality Collision Group is itself a specialty MSO with a business interest in promoting specialization over volume consolidation
The 800 closures could also reflect natural market exits (retirements, health) rather than purely competitive displacement by consolidators

claims.text: The top 3 US collision repair consolidators (Caliber, Boyd/Gerber, Crash Champions) held approximately 27% market share in 2024 and are forecast to reach 37% by 2029, confirming active market consolidation — but the Big 5 disproportionately hold revenue share (31.7%) vs. location share (13.3%), indicating that scale drives revenue density (higher throughput per shop) more than pure location-count growth.
claims.evidence: Romans Group 2024 market profile projected top-3 consolidator growth from 27% to 37% market share by 2029 over 5 years. Focus Advisors mid-2025 data confirmed the Big 5 at 4,019 locations with 31.7% revenue share vs. 13.3% location share. This 2.4x revenue-to-location ratio suggests consolidated shops run materially higher throughput than the industry average — consistent with DRP volume steering and larger physical footprints (12,000 sq ft vs. independent 6,000 sq ft average per Matthews/dealer body shop data).

citations.title: The Romans Group Releases 2024 Profile – Body Shop Business
citations.content_snippet: The Romans Group's five-year U.S. forecast has the top 3 consolidators aggressively growing. It is expected that by 2029, the top 3 consolidators will grow from their 2024 market share of over 27% to a market share of up to 37%.

citations.title: 2025 Mid-Year Review: Consolidation Continues Despite Headwinds – Focus Advisors Automotive
citations.content_snippet: The Big 5 now operate approximately 4,019 locations, collectively holding 13.3% of shop market share and approximately 31.7% of revenue market share nationwide. At the end of 2024, that revenue share was just 30%, underscoring that the Big 5 continue to extract value from prior acquisitions.

caveats: Revenue share growing faster than location share may reflect DRP insurer steering rather than superior unit economics — the volume may come at compressed margins
The 37% 2029 forecast is Romans Group's projection, not a stated operator target, and could be directionally correct without being precise
Gerber/Joe Hudson's combined entity at 1,301 locations inflates the 2025 Big 5 count significantly due to the acquisition, potentially overstating organic consolidation momentum

claims.text: Healthcare services PE roll-ups, the closest structural analogue to collision repair (fragmented, insurer-intermediated, local labor, high capex), achieve documented G&A synergy gains of 200–300 basis points within two years post-acquisition through shared back-office functions — providing an order-of-magnitude cross-check for collision repair's G&A leverage estimates and confirming the 200–400bps range is directionally realistic.
claims.evidence: Healthcare PE roll-ups (urgent care, dental, dermatology) consistently achieve 200–300bps EBITDA margin improvement in the first two years from shared revenue cycle, HR, supply purchasing, and IT. Large dental platforms trade at 9–11x EBITDA vs. 5–7x for add-ons. Urgent care large platforms at 10–15x vs. 6–11x single-site — a 4–500bps EBITDA multiple spread attributable to infrastructure and margin. Median healthcare services EV/EBITDA moderated to ~11.5x in 2024–2025, a comparable reference point for collision repair's 12–14x PE-raise valuations.

citations.title: Healthcare Roll-Ups: PE Strategy Faces New Pressures – Opus Connect
citations.content_snippet: Typical PE underwriting assumes 15–20% annual EBITDA growth through a mix of organic expansion, new site openings, and integration of ancillary services. Investors anticipate synergy gains from shared back-office functions — including revenue cycle, HR, supply purchasing, and IT — which can yield margin improvements of 200–300 basis points within the first two years post-acquisition.

citations.title: Urgent Care Practice Valuation Benchmarks – FOCUS Bankers
citations.content_snippet: Well-run urgent care centers frequently achieve EBITDA margins in the 15%–25% range. The valuation gap between a single-site operator and a scaled platform can exceed 400–500 basis points of EBITDA multiple. Large platforms with value-based care or tech-driven models can command 10x to 15x EBITDA.

caveats: Healthcare roll-ups face structurally different reimbursement dynamics (CPT codes, Medicare/Medicaid rate-setting) vs. collision repair's insurer DRP model — analogy is directional, not precise
Healthcare roll-ups have faced significant scrutiny and distress (Envision, AmSurg, TeamHealth) where leverage + insurer pressure led to bankruptcy — a cautionary parallel for collision repair
The 200–300bps G&A synergy timeline (2 years) may be faster in healthcare (which has more codified billing processes) than in collision repair (where each shop is a physical operation)

claims.text: Restaurant chain economics provide a second analogous industry validation: highly franchised restaurant systems achieve 3.5x the earnings per dollar of sales compared to low-franchise operators, with food cost management programs delivering 2–4% net margin improvement — confirming that multi-unit service businesses with centralized procurement and shared G&A can generate order-of-magnitude improvements in unit economics at scale, but only if the business model genuinely standardizes operations (franchising) rather than loosely aggregating semi-independent locations.
claims.evidence: Aaron Allen & Associates data shows highly franchised restaurants earn a median of 9.4 cents per dollar of sales vs. 2.7 cents for low-franchise operators — a 3.5x margin multiple. Food cost management programs improve restaurant margins 2–4%. The key analogy: collision repair chains that behave more like franchised systems (standardized parts procurement, centralized estimating, unified DRP relationships) should exhibit similar scale benefits to franchised restaurant systems; chains that allow shops to operate semi-independently (as many large MSOs do immediately post-acquisition) will not. This distinction explains why Boyd Group at 987 shops earns only 11% EBITDA margin vs. the 14% targeted for a well-integrated 3-shop MSO.

citations.title: Restaurant EBITDA: A Comparison of U.S. Public Companies – Aaron Allen & Associates
citations.content_snippet: For every dollar in sales, highly franchised restaurants keep a median of 9.4 cents in earnings — that's 3.5 times the margin for restaurants with less than a third of their business franchised, illustrating dramatic G&A and overhead leverage at scale.

citations.title: Restaurant Profitability Statistics – Restroworks
citations.content_snippet: Comprehensive food cost management typically improves overall restaurant profit margins by 2–4% — significant in an industry with typically single-digit net profitability. Integrated approaches allow leading restaurants to achieve margins 2–3 times industry averages.

caveats: Restaurant franchising is structurally different from collision repair company-owned multi-unit operations — the capital structure, labor model, and procurement centralization mechanisms are distinct
The restaurant analogy breaks down on insurer intermediation: restaurants serve end consumers directly, while collision repair shops' pricing is largely dictated by third-party DRP agreements
Highly franchised restaurant chains benefit from franchisee capital investment and risk, which is not available in owned collision repair platforms

claims.text: Middle market PE-backed companies at 7x+ leverage face materially elevated distress risk: at a 10% EBITDA decline and 50bps rate increase, over 25% of firms fall below 1x interest coverage, and severe stress (20% EBITDA decline) pushes distress to 40% — creating systemic risk for highly leveraged collision repair platforms if same-store revenue headwinds persist beyond 2025.
claims.evidence: ABF Journal's leverage stress analysis (2025) documented: average middle-market first-lien leverage at 4.5x debt/EBITDA as of September 2024; credit estimate population hitting 7x leverage in 2024; 20% of companies already below 1x EBITDA interest coverage. S&P's stress scenarios: base (4.5% rates, 3% EBITDA growth) = 5.5x sustainable; adverse (5% rates, -10% EBITDA) = 25% of firms below 1x; severe (5.5% rates, -20% EBITDA) = 40% in distress. For Caliber specifically: estimated ~$880M EBITDA at ~5.2x debt/EBITDA ($4.6B debt), a 20% EBITDA decline to $700M would push debt/EBITDA to 6.6x and interest coverage to approximately 2.0x — stressed but not immediately distressed at current rates.

citations.title: Leverage Limits: Stress-Testing Middle Market Debt Capacity – ABF Journal
citations.content_snippet: Middle market first-lien debt averaged 4.5x leverage as of September 2024. The middle market credit estimate population hit 7x leverage in 2024, with 20% of companies below 1x EBITDA interest coverage. S&P's mild stress scenario — a 10% EBITDA drop and a 50-basis-point rate hike — pushes over 25% of firms below 1x interest coverage.

caveats: The ABF Journal data covers all middle-market companies, not collision repair specifically — sector-specific leverage profiles may differ
Caliber's EBITDA estimate is unaudited and based on industry comparables; actual coverage ratios require non-public financial data
DRP agreements provide some revenue stability that other industries lack — insurer-backed volume may buffer EBITDA volatility relative to consumer-discretionary businesses

claims.text: Boyd Group's Project 360 — a $100M annual recurring cost savings program launched in Q4 2024 in partnership with a global consulting firm — specifically targets leveraging scale for better vendor discount structures and fewer supplier relationships, providing the most direct public-company evidence that documented scale procurement advantages at 1,000+ locations remain incompletely captured and are a management priority, not a baseline already fully realized.
claims.evidence: Boyd's Q4 2024 earnings release disclosed Project 360's $100M targeted savings, with $20–23M in upfront transition costs. Management explicitly stated the focus is on 'structural costs' and 'leveraging the size and scale we have to get better discount structures with vendors, and better positioning with a fewer number of partners.' At $3.1B in revenue, $100M represents 322bps of EBITDA improvement — suggesting that even a 987-location platform had not yet fully realized its procurement and G&A scale economics as of 2024.

citations.title: Boyd Group Services Inc. Reports Fourth Quarter and Full Year 2024 Results
citations.content_snippet: Project 360, a company-wide transformational cost initiative launched in Q4 2024 in partnership with a leading global consulting firm, is expected to result in $100 million in annual recurring cost savings over the plan period. The cost savings focus on structural costs that we can take out of the business, plus leveraging the size and scale we have to get better discount structures with vendors, and better positioning with a fewer number of partners.

caveats: Project 360 targets are forward-looking estimates, not realized savings — execution risk is real
The $100M savings mix between procurement and G&A is not disclosed, making it difficult to attribute separately

That Boyd is only now pursuing this optimization at 987 locations implies earlier roll-up phases did not systematically capture scale benefits — a warning for smaller platforms claiming similar advantages

claims.text: The prevailing acquisition market multiple for collision repair transactions was approximately 7.0x EBITDA in 2025, representing a meaningful compression from the 12–14x PE-raise valuations, and creating a 5–7x multiple gap between PE capital-raise and market exit — which is only bridge-able if: (a) EBITDA grows materially post-acquisition, (b) a public market exit (Caliber IPO) reprices the sector at a premium, or (c) a strategic acquirer pays a control premium above market.
claims.evidence: Focus Advisors' 2025 year-in-review reported a prevailing acquisition multiple of 7.0x EBITDA, described as 'relatively stable year-over-year' despite the 2024 headwinds. The 12–14x PE-raise valuation is documented across multiple sources. The 5–7x multiple gap means PE investors need EBITDA growth of approximately 70–100% (from buy-side to raise-side EBITDA base) for the multiple arbitrage to generate adequate returns — a challenge if same-store revenue is declining. Caliber Holdings filed confidentially for an IPO in July 2025, which if completed, would provide the first public market pricing benchmark for a 1,800+ location platform.

citations.title: Year in Review 2025: Slowdown, and Then a Blockbuster – Focus Advisors Automotive
citations.content_snippet: Prevailing acquisition multiple: 7.0x EBITDA. Multiples described as relatively stable year-over-year; a narrower band of valuations across deals. Buying strong single shops and small MSOs at five to seven times EBITDA while raising capital at valuations of 12 to 14 times allows this new capital to effectively leverage their superior capital into faster growth.

citations.title: Caliber Files Confidential Draft Registration Statement for Proposed IPO – CollisionWeek
citations.content_snippet: On July 28, 2025, Caliber Holdings Inc. confidentially submitted a draft registration statement (Form S-1) to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a proposed initial public offering. The number of shares and price range have not yet been determined.

caveats: 7x market multiple reflects conditions in 2025 when revenue was under pressure — in a recovery environment, multiples could normalize to 8–9x
The 12–14x raise-side valuation may embed a liquidity/control premium that is not directly comparable to transaction multiples for add-on acquisitions
The Caliber IPO, if completed, could set a new public market anchor for the sector that either validates or challenges the PE-raise valuations

claims.text: The scale economy benefits of collision repair consolidation — while real and documented — are insufficient on their own to justify 12–14x acquisition multiples under base-case 2024–2025 market conditions, because the observed EBITDA margin gap between large platforms and independents (approximately 5% at small MSO scale, potentially 6–8% at 500+ locations) produces incremental value that, when capitalized at the market's own current 7x EBITDA multiple, implies incremental enterprise value per dollar of EBITDA well below the implied premium in PE-raise valuations.
claims.evidence: The math: a 500-shop platform at 15% EBITDA vs. 500 independents at 9% EBITDA generates 6% more EBITDA per dollar of revenue. If each shop runs $3M revenue, the platform generates $450M revenue × 15% = $67.5M platform EBITDA vs. the same shops as independents generating $450M × 9% = $40.5M. The incremental $27M EBITDA at 7x market multiple = $189M additional enterprise value — consistent with a 10x overall multiple (vs. 7x for independents × $40.5M = $283.5M). But PE raise at 12–14x: $40.5M × 14x = $567M raise-side value vs. $283.5M independent value = 2x multiple expansion expected. The 6% margin improvement only justifies approximately 10x total platform multiple; the 12–14x PE-raise requires either multiple re-rating (Caliber IPO) or EBITDA growth beyond scale economics alone.

citations.title: Growing the Independent MSO: Create More Value by Scaling Up – Focus Advisors Automotive
citations.content_snippet: A single shop might be valued at 3X to 3.5X EBITDA, whereas a medium MSO would realize a multiple closer to 5X to 5.5X. By increasing revenues by 200% (from $3M to $9M), an owner could ultimately grow the value of the business by around 633%.

citations.title: Year in Review 2025: Slowdown, and Then a Blockbuster – Focus Advisors Automotive
citations.content_snippet: Market multiples remained relatively stable at approximately 7x EBITDA throughout 2025, meaning buyers did not change what they were willing to pay on a multiple basis. Shop earnings, not buyer appetite, drove purchase prices down.

caveats: This analysis uses public market (7x) as the discount rate for incremental EBITDA — PE exits may occur at 10–12x public market or strategic multiples that make 12–14x raise valuations more defensible
The 6% incremental EBITDA margin estimate is itself uncertain and model-derived
Roll-up arbitrage has historically generated strong returns in analogous industries (dental, veterinary, HVAC) even at similar multiple spreads — collision repair may follow the same pattern

claims.text: Parts sourcing in collision repair is split approximately 62% OEM, 22% aftermarket, and 10% recycled — and the growing mandate for OEM parts in ADAS-equipped and EV repairs (90%+ OEM for EV repairs) is shifting the mix toward the highest-cost, lowest-discount part type, compressing the blended procurement advantage available to large chains and limiting the practical cost reduction from LKQ-type alternative parts sourcing as the vehicle parc modernizes.
claims.evidence: Industry sources confirm the current parts mix: OEM 62%, aftermarket 22%, recycled 10%. EV collision repairs require 90%+ OEM parts. ADAS technology is present in over 92% of new US vehicles. The average parts per repair order grew from 9 (2018) to 14 (2023) — more parts, but skewing toward OEM on complex ADAS repairs. Insurer mandates and OEM certification program requirements are reinforcing the OEM mix. This trend structurally limits the value of LKQ recycled/aftermarket discounts (50–70% below OEM) as those categories shrink as a share of the total parts bill.

citations.title: Collision Repair Industry to Be Influenced by Supply Chain, Vehicle Complexity in 2024 – Autobody News
citations.content_snippet: OEM parts market share in collision repair is 62%, aftermarket parts usage accounts for 22% of total parts spend, and recycled (salvage) parts represent 10% of the total parts mix. The average number of parts per repair order increased from 9 in 2018 to 14 in 2023.

citations.title: Scale Is Not Strategy: The Collision Repair Consolidation Crisis – Quality Collision Group
citations.content_snippet: EV repairs require over 90% OEM parts. Calibration systems cost up to $500,000 per location. Newer models require OEM components and ADAS calibrations, producing a bifurcated sourcing landscape.

caveats: The OEM mandate trend may be partially offset by growing OEM wholesale discount programs targeted at large MSOs — major OEMs have begun offering certified collision network programs with preferred pricing
The 62/22/10 mix may not accurately reflect the current year; ADAS-mandated OEM mix may have already pushed OEM share higher in 2024–2025
Aftermarket parts quality and ADAS-compatibility certification are improving, potentially allowing greater non-OEM penetration than current mandates suggest

claims.text: 130+ PE firms had expressed interest in the collision repair sector as of 2024–2025, and the industry received over $9 billion in capital (primarily debt refinancing) across six major transactions in an 18-month window — representing a supply-of-capital dynamic that may sustain elevated acquisition multiples independent of demonstrated scale economics, creating a potential valuation bubble disconnected from fundamental EBITDA performance.
claims.evidence: Focus Advisors confirmed 130+ PE firms expressing platform interest across two years of conversations. Over $9B in capital entered the industry from November 2023 to mid-2024 across six major transactions. PE firms' AUM exceeds $400B across the collision repair sponsor universe. Three new PE firms entered in H1 2025 despite the industry headwinds. This capital supply dynamic means acquisition multiples are partly driven by competitive dynamics among capital allocators, not just by fundamental EBITDA performance at target companies.

citations.title: 2024 Year in Review: Some Excel on a Bumpy Road – Focus Advisors Automotive
citations.content_snippet: Focus Advisors said it spoke with more firms in 2024 than ever before, and currently has a list of more than 130 PE firms that have expressed interest in entering the industry. Until early 2024, private equity firms would only consider partnering with owners of platforms that had five or more locations and $20M+ in revenue. The big chunk was $4.6 billion in debt refinancing by Caliber Collision.

citations.title: Billions and Billions: Private Equity Investments in Collision Repair Surge – Body Shop Business
citations.content_snippet: In the last five months, more than $9 billion in capital was invested into the collision repair industry by PE firms. Collectively, the AUM of all PE sponsors in collision repair exceeds $400 billion. Buying strong single shops and small MSOs at five to seven times EBITDA while raising capital at valuations of 12 to 14 times allows this capital to effectively leverage into faster growth.

caveats: Capital supply alone cannot sustain multiples indefinitely — lender covenants and LP performance accountability will force discipline if EBITDA performance does not support debt service
The $9B figure is dominated by Caliber's $4.6B refinancing (a recapitalization/dividend transaction, not an acquisition), which inflates the headline capital-deployment figure
Some PE interest may be speculative or exploratory; actual committed capital to new platforms is substantially less than the 130+ firm interest list implies

absence_report: Specific proprietary volume discount tier structures from Axalta, BASF (Glasurit/R-M), and PPG Industries for MSO programs at 50, 100, 500, and 1,000+ location thresholds — suppliers do not publicly disclose these and no industry source quantified the tier breakpoints above the small-MSO (3-shop) level documented by Focus Advisors

Caliber Collision's actual audited financial statements — revenue, EBITDA, EBITDA margin, interest expense, and net income/loss — for FY2024 or any recent period, as the company is privately held and its S-1 remains confidential; all Caliber financial estimates in this report are extrapolated from shop count, industry peers (Boyd), and management commentary

G&A as a percentage of revenue at specific shop-count thresholds (5, 50, 500+) for any collision repair operator; no operator publicly discloses this breakdown, and the estimates provided are triangulated from observed EBITDA improvement and analogous service industry data

Quantified DRP margin impact — the specific percentage by which DRP participation reduces net EBITDA margins relative to non-DRP work, or the percentage of scale procurement savings captured by insurers vs. retained by shops; this is the most analytically significant gap for the multiple-justification question

Crash Champions' financial data — revenue, EBITDA, EBITDA margin, and debt profile post-recapitalization — as the third-largest US consolidator; only Boyd Group data is publicly available as the only large pure-play public company

Independent vs. MSO financial comparison on a same-market, same-vintage basis — all comparative data comes from advisory sources with roll-up promotion incentives; no independent academic or regulatory study of MSO vs. independent unit economics was found

Incremental procurement cost data for platform operators above 100 locations — the documented data point range only covers single-shop to 3-shop MSO; the extrapolation to 500+ locations is modeled, not documented

Labor rate concessions in DRP contracts — no source quantified the specific percentage below market rate that DRP-participating shops accept, or the distribution of this discount across insurer programs (State Farm, GEICO, Progressive, Allstate, etc.)

OEM manufacturer (not dealer) volume discount programs for large collision chains — emerging programs by Ford, GM, Toyota, etc. for preferred collision network pricing were referenced qualitatively but not quantified
Total loss rate by vehicle type and age in the top 10 MSAs, which would allow geographic differentiation of where scale economics are most defensible vs. most challenged

EBITDA margin data for mid-tier MSOs (10–100 locations) to fill the gap between the documented 3-shop (14%) and 987-shop Boyd (11%) data points — the absence of this data prevents a clean scale curve construction

Audited per-shop revenue, EBITDA, parts cost, and labor cost data from any large-chain operator — Boyd Group provides consolidated figures but not per-location breakdowns, preventing unit-level verification of scale benefits
